title: Introducing Smell-O-Vision!
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore Smell-O-Vision, the 1950s-60s attempt to accompany films with synchronized scents. They trace early precedents (Roxy Rothafel's Family Theater rose-oil experiment, 1939-40 Scentovision at the New York World's Fair by Hans Laube and Robert Barthes), the role of Michael Todd Jr. and his 1957-era Smell-O-Vision system, the 1960 film Scent of Mystery and its flop, Walter Reade Jr.'s Aroma-Rama, and later attempts such as John Waters' Polyester scratch-and-sniff card, the Censorium and 4-D theaters (4DX), and home scent systems. The episode closes with a listener thank-you email.

entities.name: Around the World in Eighty Days

segments.title: Cotton candy banter and show opening
segments.summary: Hosts open with chat about cotton candy and childhood cotton candy machines, then introduce the Smell-O-Vision topic.

segments.title: Smell-O-Vision overview and sources
segments.summary: Smell-O-Vision is introduced as a 1960s gimmick to pair scents with motion pictures. Sources include Patrick Kaiger's book Popular Americana and a Martin J. Smith LA Times article. Time listed the idea among its worst inventions of the century.

segments.title: Early scent in theaters and Roxy Rothafel
segments.summary: Scent was used in stage productions in the 1800s. Roxy Rothafel's Family Theater in Forest City, Pennsylvania piped in rose oil in 1916 alongside a newsreel of the Rose Bowl Parade. Other theaters tried scent in Boston in 1929 and Detroit in 1943.

segments.title: Hans Laube and Scentovision at the World's Fair
segments.summary: Swiss inventor and osmologist Hans Laube, known for removing odors, debuted Scentovision at the 1939-40 New York World's Fair with partner Robert Barthes, using a 35-minute film with 32 chemical odors. The New York Times endorsed it, though the projectionist also ran the scents.

segments.title: Postwar TV pressure and Michael Todd Jr.
segments.summary: After World War Two, theater owners faced competition from TV and tried novelties like Smell-O-Vision. Michael Todd Jr. took up the project after his father's film success with Around the World in Eighty Days; Michael Todd Sr. was born Avrom Hirsch Goldbogen. Todd Sr. died in a plane crash in 1958.
topics: Around the World in Eighty Days

segments.title: Scent of Mystery and the smell brain mechanism
segments.summary: Laube and Todd Jr. developed Scent of Mystery as the first film scripted around smells. The contract required the name change to Smell-O-Vision. The 'smell brain' used a motorized belt of chemical vials and a needle to release scents into a fan and tubing.

segments.title: Aroma-Rama competitor and critical reception
segments.summary: Walter Reade Jr. beat them to market with Aroma-Rama at the Demille Theater in New York, using the documentary Behind the Great Wall. The New York Times panned the smells and the film, and the review also mentioned the upcoming Scent of Mystery.

segments.title: Scent of Mystery premiere and flop
segments.summary: Scent of Mystery, directed by Jack Cardiff and starring Peter Lorre and Denholm Elliott, was set in Spain with smell-linked plot points. Reviews were poor and Laube's daughter Carmen claimed the system was under-built, without tubing under each seat. The planned expansion to 100 theaters was canceled and Laube died in debt.

segments.title: Aftermath for Todd Jr. and Laube, Best Air
segments.summary: Todd Jr. produced no further films; two trademarked scripts, Bumpkin's Holiday and Creature from the Bronx, were never made. Laube's earlier air freshener invention, Best Air, also failed.

segments.title: Later scent gimmicks: John Waters and Rugrats
segments.summary: John Waters' 1981 film Polyester came with a scratch-and-sniff card, and the 2003 Rugrats Go Wild included a similar gag.

segments.title: Censorium, 4DX and four-D theaters
segments.summary: The Censorium opened in 1984 at Six Flags Power Plant in Baltimore, with moving seats, smells, water spray and popcorn scents. It closed in 1990. The South Korean 4DX system began in 2009 with about 21 effects, and Josh cites a Quartz review that found the seat punches distracting. Sammy Smart enjoyed 4DX for Top Gun.

segments.title: Home scent systems and Holiday in Spain
segments.summary: Spanish company Olorama sells a home scent device holding up to 20 smells, syncing with movies via software. The hosts compare it to the old iSmell peripheral. The 1960 film was re-released as Holiday in Spain with the smell parts removed, which made it seem surreal.

segments.title: Listener mail from Emily
segments.summary: Emily writes about listening to the show for about ten years and using it to fall asleep, through grad school, career start, grief and sobriety. Josh gives the email address stuff podcast at iHeartRadio dot com.
